concepts.title: Self-Similarity: Patterns All the Way Down
concepts.contentHtml:
A fractal is a shape that looks similar at every scale. Zoom in, and you see smaller copies of the whole shape. Zoom in again -- more copies.

This property is called self-similarity. Unlike a circle (which looks like a straight line when you zoom in), a fractal never smooths out. It has infinite detail at every magnification.

The word "fractal" was coined by Benoit Mandelbrot in 1975, from the Latin fractus meaning "broken" or "fragmented."

concepts.title: Fractals in Nature
concepts.contentHtml:
Nature is full of fractal-like structures:

Coastlines: The coast of Britain looks jagged at every scale -- from satellite view to walking along it. Mandelbrot asked: "How long is the coast of Britain?" The answer depends on your ruler!

Ferns: Each frond of a fern contains smaller fronds, which contain even smaller ones.
Broccoli: Romanesco broccoli is a stunning natural fractal -- each bud is a miniature version of the whole.
Lightning: Branching patterns repeat at smaller and smaller scales.
Rivers: River networks branch like trees, with tributaries branching into sub-tributaries.

concepts.title: Fractal Dimension
concepts.contentHtml:
A line is 1-dimensional. A square is 2-dimensional. But a fractal can have a dimension between integers!

The fractal dimension measures how completely a fractal fills space. The Koch curve has dimension log(4)/log(3) ≈ 1.26 -- more than a line but less than a plane.

Intuitively: the Koch curve is "too wiggly" to be a line, but "too thin" to be a surface. Fractal dimension captures this precisely.

concepts.title: Construction: Remove the Middle
concepts.contentHtml:
Start with a solid equilateral triangle. Find the midpoints of each side and connect them -- this creates 4 smaller triangles. Remove the middle one.

Now repeat: for each of the 3 remaining triangles, find the midpoints, connect them, remove the middle. Repeat forever.

What remains is the Sierpinski triangle (or Sierpinski gasket) -- a fractal made of 3 copies of itself, each scaled to half size.

concepts.title: Three Ways to Build It
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sierpinski triangle can be constructed in remarkably different ways that all give the same shape:

1. Geometric removal: Start with a triangle, repeatedly remove midpoint triangles (as above).

2. Chaos game: Pick a random point inside a triangle. Repeatedly jump halfway toward a randomly chosen vertex. The trail of points forms the Sierpinski triangle!

3. Pascal's triangle mod 2: Write out Pascal's triangle and color odd numbers. The pattern of odd entries IS the Sierpinski triangle. This connection between algebra and geometry is deep and beautiful.

concepts.title: Dimension of the Sierpinski Triangle
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sierpinski triangle is made of 3 copies of itself, each scaled by a factor of 1/2.

For a normal shape, if you scale by 1/2 in D dimensions you get (1/2)^D = 1/N copies. So N = 2^D, which gives D = log(N)/log(2).

For the Sierpinski triangle: 3 = 2^D, so D = log(3)/log(2) ≈ 1.585.

It has dimension between 1 and 2 -- more than a line, but it has zero area (we removed it all!). It fills space more than a curve but less than a surface.

title: The Mandelbrot Set
description: The most famous fractal in mathematics

concepts.title: The Iteration z → z² + c
concepts.contentHtml:
The Mandelbrot set is defined by an astonishingly simple rule. For each complex number c, iterate:

z₀ = 0, z₁ = z₀² + c, z₂ = z₁² + c, ...

If the sequence stays bounded (never escapes to infinity), then c is in the Mandelbrot set. If it escapes, c is outside.

For example: c = 0 gives 0, 0, 0, ... (bounded -- in the set). c = 1 gives 0, 1, 2, 5, 26, ... (escapes -- not in the set). c = -1 gives 0, -1, 0, -1, ... (bounded -- in the set).

concepts.title: Escape Time and Coloring
concepts.contentHtml:
Points outside the Mandelbrot set escape to infinity at different speeds. We can color them by how quickly they escape -- this produces the stunning images you have seen.

A key theorem: if |z| ever exceeds 2, the sequence will definitely escape to infinity. So we iterate up to some maximum and check whether |z| > 2.

Points that escape quickly are colored one way, points that take longer another, and points that never escape (the set itself) are colored black. This escape-time algorithm creates the iconic fractal imagery.

concepts.title: Infinite Complexity at the Boundary
concepts.contentHtml:
The boundary of the Mandelbrot set is infinitely complex. No matter how far you zoom, you find new structures -- spirals, tendrils, miniature copies of the whole set (called "mini-brots").

The set is connected (one piece) but its boundary has infinite length. Its boundary has fractal dimension 2 -- as complicated as a boundary can possibly be!

Despite being generated by the simple rule z → z² + c, the Mandelbrot set contains more detail than any human could explore in a lifetime. It has been called "the most complex object in mathematics."

concepts.title: Julia Sets: Varying the Starting Point
concepts.contentHtml:
While the Mandelbrot set fixes z₀ = 0 and varies c, a Julia set does the opposite: it fixes c and varies the starting point z₀.

For a given c, the filled Julia set K_c is the set of all z₀ values whose orbits under z → z² + c stay bounded.

Each value of c gives a completely different Julia set. Some are connected, lacy patterns. Others are disconnected clouds of points called Fatou dust. The variety is breathtaking.
mathExpressions: K_c = \{z_0 \in \mathbb{C} : z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c \text{ stays bounded}\}

concepts.title: Connected vs. Disconnected
concepts.contentHtml:
Fatou's theorem gives a beautiful dichotomy: for each c, the Julia set is either completely connected (one piece) or totally disconnected (a Cantor-like dust of infinitely many points, none touching).

There is nothing in between -- no Julia set has exactly 2 pieces, or 17 pieces. It is all or nothing!

Famous connected Julia sets: c = -0.7 + 0.27i (a swirling dragon), c = -0.123 + 0.745i (the "Douady rabbit" with three-fold symmetry), c = -1 (the basilica, shaped like linked circles).

concepts.title: The Mandelbrot-Julia Connection
concepts.contentHtml:
There is a profound relationship between the Mandelbrot set and Julia sets:

c is in the Mandelbrot set if and only if the Julia set for c is connected.

So the Mandelbrot set is a "map" of all Julia sets! Each point in the Mandelbrot set corresponds to a connected Julia set. Each point outside corresponds to a disconnected one (Fatou dust).

Points near the boundary of the Mandelbrot set give the most intricate Julia sets. The Mandelbrot set is, in a deep sense, an index of all possible Julia sets.

concepts.title: Deterministic but Unpredictable
concepts.contentHtml:
Chaos is one of the most surprising discoveries in mathematics: simple, deterministic rules can produce behavior that is effectively unpredictable.

A chaotic system has no randomness -- given exact initial conditions, the future is completely determined. But sensitive dependence on initial conditions means that tiny differences in starting values grow exponentially over time.

Two trajectories starting 0.0001 apart can end up completely different after enough iterations. Since we can never measure initial conditions with infinite precision, long-term prediction becomes impossible.

concepts.title: The Butterfly Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1963, meteorologist Edward Lorenz discovered chaos by accident. Running a weather simulation, he re-entered a value rounded from 0.506127 to 0.506. The tiny difference -- 0.000127 -- led to completely different weather!

He famously asked: "Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?" This became known as the butterfly effect.

Lorenz's discovery shook science: it showed that even perfect physical laws cannot guarantee long-term prediction. Weather forecasts become unreliable beyond about 10 days, not because of bad models, but because of chaos itself.

concepts.title: The Logistic Map: Simple Rule, Complex Behavior
concepts.contentHtml:
The logistic map is perhaps the simplest chaotic system:

x_{n+1} = r * x_n * (1 - x_n)

This models population growth: x is the population (between 0 and 1), and r is the growth rate. Despite its simplicity, this one equation produces an astonishing range of behavior:

For r < 3: the population settles to a stable value.
For r ≈ 3.45: it oscillates between 2 values.
For r ≈ 3.54: it oscillates between 4 values.
For r ≈ 3.57 and beyond: chaos -- the population bounces unpredictably forever.

concepts.title: Period Doubling Cascade
concepts.contentHtml:
As r increases in the logistic map x → rx(1-x), the system undergoes a remarkable sequence of period-doubling bifurcations:

At r ≈ 3.0: the stable fixed point splits into a 2-cycle (oscillation between two values).
At r ≈ 3.449: the 2-cycle splits into a 4-cycle.
At r ≈ 3.544: the 4-cycle becomes an 8-cycle.
The doublings come faster and faster, accumulating at r ≈ 3.5699...

Beyond this accumulation point lies chaos -- but with surprising "windows" of order where periodic behavior briefly returns.

concepts.title: Feigenbaum's Universal Constant
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1975, Mitchell Feigenbaum discovered something astonishing. The ratio of successive bifurcation intervals converges to a universal constant:

δ ≈ 4.6692016091...

Each period-doubling happens roughly 4.669 times faster than the previous one. The stunning part: this same constant appears in every system that undergoes period doubling -- not just the logistic map!

Feigenbaum's constant is as fundamental as π or e. It appears in fluid dynamics, electronic circuits, lasers, and chemical reactions. It is a universal law of the route to chaos.

concepts.title: The Bifurcation Diagram
concepts.contentHtml:
The bifurcation diagram plots the long-term behavior of the logistic map for each value of r. It is one of the most famous images in all of mathematics.

On the left (small r): a single line showing the stable fixed point. Then the line forks into two (period-2), then four, then eight... The forkings accumulate into a region of chaos -- a dense cloud of points.

But look carefully within the chaos: there are windows of order! At r ≈ 3.83, a period-3 cycle suddenly appears. The mathematician Li and Yorke proved: "Period three implies chaos" -- if a system has a 3-cycle, it has cycles of every period.

concepts.title: The Lorenz Attractor
concepts.contentHtml:
When Lorenz modeled atmospheric convection, he discovered that the trajectories of his system trace out a beautiful butterfly-shaped object in 3D space: the Lorenz attractor.

A strange attractor is a set toward which a chaotic system evolves over time. No matter where you start, the trajectory is pulled toward the attractor -- but once there, it wanders chaotically, never exactly repeating.

The Lorenz attractor has two "wings." The trajectory spirals around one wing, then unpredictably switches to the other, then back -- like a butterfly's wings. The exact sequence of switches is chaotic.

concepts.title: Fractal Dimension of Attractors
concepts.contentHtml:
Strange attractors have fractal dimension. The Lorenz attractor has dimension ≈ 2.06 -- slightly more than a surface, because the trajectory folds and stretches in complex ways.

This fractal structure arises from stretching and folding: the dynamics stretch nearby trajectories apart (chaos) while folding them back into a bounded region (the attractor). This is like kneading dough -- pulling apart and folding over creates layers within layers.

The fractal dimension tells us the effective number of degrees of freedom in the chaotic system. A dimension of 2.06 means the attractor almost fills a surface but has a finely layered internal structure.

concepts.title: More Strange Attractors
concepts.contentHtml:
The Hénon map is a 2D map: x → 1 - ax² + y, y → bx. With a = 1.4, b = 0.3, it produces a strange attractor with dimension ≈ 1.26 -- a fractal curve made of infinitely many nested curves.

The Rössler attractor is simpler than Lorenz's: it has a single spiral that folds back on itself. It helped scientists understand how stretching and folding generate chaos.

Strange attractors appear everywhere in nature: turbulent fluid flows, heart rhythms, population dynamics, and even the orbit of Pluto (which is technically chaotic, though stable for billions of years).

concepts.title: L-Systems: Growing Fractals with Grammar
concepts.contentHtml:
Lindenmayer systems (L-systems) model plant growth using simple grammar rules. Start with a string (axiom) and repeatedly apply substitution rules.

Example -- a simple tree:
Axiom: F
Rule: F → F[+F]F[-F]F

Interpret F as "draw forward," + as "turn left," - as "turn right," [ as "save position," ] as "restore position." After a few iterations, this produces realistic branching trees!

L-systems can generate ferns, flowers, shrubs, and even entire ecosystems. They show that complex organic forms arise from simple recursive rules.

concepts.title: Fractal Technology
concepts.contentHtml:
Fractal antennas exploit self-similarity to operate at multiple frequencies simultaneously. Your cell phone likely contains a fractal antenna -- its branching shape lets it receive calls, WiFi, Bluetooth, and GPS with a single compact component.

Fractal compression stores images by finding self-similar patterns. Instead of storing every pixel, it stores the transformations that generate the image. This can achieve very high compression ratios for natural images.

Fractals also appear in computer graphics (generating realistic mountains, clouds, and coastlines), medicine (analyzing blood vessel branching and lung structure), and finance (modeling stock market fluctuations).

concepts.title: Fractals, Art, and Deep Mathematics
concepts.contentHtml:
Studies of Jackson Pollock's drip paintings found that they have fractal dimension, ranging from about 1.1 in his early works to 1.7 in later ones. His technique of dripping and splattering naturally created multi-scale patterns.

The Cantor set -- formed by repeatedly removing the middle third of a line segment -- connects fractals to deep number theory. It has dimension log(2)/log(3) ≈ 0.631 and is uncountably infinite despite having zero length!

Fractals reveal that complexity need not arise from complex rules. The Mandelbrot set comes from z → z² + c. The Sierpinski triangle comes from removing middles. Chaos comes from x → rx(1-x). Simple iteration, repeated endlessly, creates infinite beauty.
